stimulus.text:
| Place | Action | What it did |
|---|---|---|
| Vermont | 1777 constitution | Slavery banned outright |
| Pennsylvania | 1780 law | Children born after March 1, 1780, free at age 28 |
| Massachusetts | 1783 court decisions | Slavery ended under the 1780 state constitution |
| Connecticut | 1784 law | Children born after March 1, 1784, free at age 25 |
| Rhode Island | 1784 law | Children born after March 1, 1784, free at 18 (girls) or 21 (boys) |
| New York | 1799 law | Children born after July 4, 1799, free at 28 (boys) or 25 (girls) |
| Northwest Territory | 1787 ordinance | Slavery banned in the territory |
stimulus.source_note: Compiled from state constitutions, statutes, and court decisions, 1777-1799. Public record.

books.section: Topic 3.6 The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals, A. The Call for Egalitarianism

stem: Which of the following best explains why the table's northern pattern did not spread to the South?

options.text: The Constitution of 1787 banned slavery in every state
options.misconception: The Constitution did no such thing; it protected slavery and barred Congress from ending the slave trade before 1808.

options.text: Southern slavery grew profitable after the cotton gin; northern slavery stayed small
The Northwest Ordinance required southern states to keep slavery
options.misconception: The Ordinance banned slavery only in the Northwest Territory; it required nothing of the southern states.

options.text: The French Revolution ended slavery throughout the Americas in the year 1789
options.misconception: The French Revolution did not end slavery in the Americas; Saint-Domingue's enslaved people won their own freedom by rebellion, not by French decree.

rationales.B: Northern slavery was small and mostly household labor, so gradual laws cost owners little. Background: Eli Whitney's cotton gin of 1793 made slave-grown cotton pay, so southern planters held on tighter.
rationales.A: The Constitution protected slavery; it never banned it in any state.
rationales.C: The Ordinance touched only the Northwest Territory; southern states kept slavery by their own choice.
rationales.D: No French decree ended American slavery; the Haitian Revolution was won by the enslaved themselves, not granted from Paris.
rationales.general:
1. Compare the economies. Background: northern slavery was small and household-based, so ending it cost owners little.
2. Ask what changed in the South. Background: the cotton gin of 1793 made short-staple cotton profitable, and slavery with it.
3. Judge the split. The same ideals produced gradual laws where slavery was marginal and resistance where it paid.
Remember: ideals bend toward interest — ask who profits from the old order before asking why it survives.
